questions.q: In recursive reward modeling, what does the human get before judging the harder, target task?
options: Help from an assistant model that was itself trained with ordinary reward modeling on a task the human can already judge
A larger dataset of randomly sampled outputs to compare
Access to the model's full training data
A guarantee that the target task has already been solved correctly
questions.explain: The core move in RRM is giving the human an aligned assistant from an easier task to help them evaluate a harder one, rather than asking them to judge the harder task completely unaided.

options: Because the mechanism repeats at increasing capability levels: each level's aligned assistant helps produce the next level's aligned assistant
Because the reward model must be retrained every hour during deployment
Because it requires recursive neural network architectures specifically
Because it uses the exact same training run repeated with no changes
questions.explain: The recursion is in the process, not the architecture — a level-1 assistant helps train a level-2 assistant, which helps train a level-3 assistant, and so on.

questions.q: What is the main advantage recursive reward modeling has in terms of adoption?
options: It requires an entirely new training algorithm that replaces RLHF
It reuses the existing RLHF machinery already in production, making it comparatively easy to adopt incrementally
It only works on vision models, not language models
It eliminates the need for any human involvement at any level
questions.explain: RRM builds on standard reward modeling rather than inventing a new training paradigm, which is part of why it's attractive as an incremental research direction.

questions.q: What is the central risk that compounds across iterations in recursive reward modeling?
options: The training process becomes too slow to be practical at any level
The human evaluator becomes unavailable after the first iteration
Each level requires exponentially more human evaluators than the last
A flaw in an assistant model that is invisible to the human overseeing it can get baked into the next level's reward model instead of being caught
questions.explain: Because each level depends on the previous assistant actually being aligned and helpful, an undetected flaw doesn't stay contained — it can propagate and compound through later levels.

questions.q: How does the lesson describe the relationship between recursive reward modeling and debate?
options: Recursive reward modeling requires debate to function at all
They attack the oversight problem from different angles and are often discussed as complementary, with debate potentially serving as the 'assistance' within an RRM pipeline
Debate is simply an earlier, now-abandoned version of recursive reward modeling
They are mutually exclusive techniques and only one can be used in any given pipeline
questions.explain: The lesson frames the two as complementary approaches that can be combined rather than competing options that exclude each other.
